Mulligan's Child.

The story as it reached here is as follows: John Mulligan, a prosperous farmer in Simpson county, had a handsome daughter, 14 years of age, whom he compelled to work in the field with negroes. event-1895-08-29.A4:
HANGED TO A TREE.
A Negro Charged With the Betrayal of a Planter's Daughter is Lynched.

JACKSON, Miss., Aug. 31.—John Mulligan is a prosperous farmer of Simpson county, twenty miles southeast of here.

His pretty 14-year-old daughter, who has been reared in ignorance and to work in his broad cotton fields with Negroes, became a mother Sunday. She named the author of her shame, a 21-year-old Negro farm hand, who took to the woods.

He was pursued, captured and landed in the county jail at Oustville.

Thursday he was taken from jail to be carried before a justice of the peace for a preliminary trial, but he never got there.

Mulligan's neighbors met the officers in Strong river swamp, took the prisoner and hanged him on the highest limb they could reach, where he swung 24 hours before being cut down.
event-1895-08-29.A5:
HUNG THE NEGRO. MISSISSIPPI MOB TAKES LAW IN THEIR OWN HANDS. White Girl Gives Birth to Colored Child, and Negro to Blame Is Strung Up.
Jackson, Miss., August 30.—From Mr. J. McLeod of Simpson county, who was in the city today, was learned the first particulars of a lynching that took place near Westville, Miss., in an out-of-the-way neighborhood. A few days ago the 13-year-old daughter of Thomas Mulligan, a prosperous farmer living near Westville, gave birth to a negro child and simultaneously one of the negro farm hands took to the woods. He was pursued and captured and lodged in the Westville jail until next day when the officers started with him for the Mulligan neighborhood for trial. On the way the prisoner was captured by a crowd of men and boys and was strung up to a tree in Strong river swamp.

A LEPER AT LARGE.

He Was Found at St. Louis, But Escapés.

Escapes.

St. Louis, Mo., August 30.—A leper whose malady was well defined and pronounced genuine by leading physicians and the health authorities, left St. Louis last night for parts unknown. He came here from Southern Texas six weeks ago. The disease did not show on his face or hands but was virulent under his clothing. The health authorities had no where to send him, the pest house being occupied by small pox patients. While the officers were discussing the dilemma he left town. The authorities will not give his name nor state where he lived gluring his residence in town.

Jockey Simms got into a quarrel with a Coney Island waiter, recently, and Simms knocked him down with a bottle. He was locked on.

event-2.A1:
HEARTHEOTHERSIDE

Another Review of the Pollard Murder Case.

ARE THE WOMEN GUILTY?

A Fort Mitchell Citizen Goes Over the Whole Ground.

NO DANGER OF LYNCHING.

What the Coroner's Inquest Developed—Marable's Confession—The Richmond Military and Their Cri- cism—Corroborative Testimony.
DANGER!
Having noticed many inaccuracies in your correspondence relating to the Poliard murder, and not having seen a line from any citizen of the immediate vicinity in which the murder was committed, I deem it my duty as one of the first to reach the scene of the murder and as one perfectly familiar with the case from the beginning to the end, to give a few facts as seen from the standpoint of a citizen. As stated, the writer was one of the first to reach the scene of the murder, and it would have required only a few moments to convince any man of ordinary perception beyond the shadow of doubt that the chops, hacks, and bruises on the face and head of the dead were the work of a woman.

An examination of the house revealing the fact that a bunch of keys had been taken from the bottom corner of a certain drawer, and four or five trunks and chests unlocked, their contents examined, such articles as were desired appropriated, all trunks and chests reclosed, and the keys replaced, would have said to any detective in unmistakable language that "this is the work of some person who is perfectly familiar with all the surroundings."

MARY ABERNATHY.

Mary Abernathy, the last person seen in the company of the deceased, was the first witness examined by the Coroner's jury, which was empanelled about midnight after the evening of the murder. The murder was committed about 5 o'clock. In answer to the question, whether or not she had seen any suspicious person about the place that day, she replied under oath that she had seen no one that day, "good, bad, or indifferent," and emphasized this statement by repeating it, and slapping her hands together as she did so.

It is an old adage that "children and fools tell the truth." From a little colored girl who lived in the neighborhood, and who, it was learned, had spent the day at Mary Abernathy's house, Constable E. A. Clements and the writer had learned that upon the return of Mary Abernathy from Mr. Pollard's house late in the afternoon of the day of the murder her little daughter Mary remarked: "Mamma look like she been fighting."

We also learned from the girl that Mary had said to her husband, Wilson Abernathy, "I saw that man going down the fence." Her husband asked "what man?" She answered, "that tail man." Her husband then replied, "that was Solomon."

Both Mary and her husband denied this conversation under oath, but on cross-examination (not in the presence of each other) each admitted to be true every word, as stated by the colored girl.

Why did they deny having seen Solomon? At this time he was not even suspected of being implicated in the murder.

This is given as only one of the many circumstances tending to implicate the two women in the murder.

AS TO THE DANGER OF LYNCHING.

Reports as to the danger of mob violence in the case, have been grossly exaggerated. On this point, the writer claims to be as well posted as any one else, and here emphatically state, that since the prisoners were landed in jail there had not been, at any time (with one single exception, which will be alluded to later), the slightest danger of their being lynched.

Solomon Marable, the last one of the three murderers captured, was caught at Five Forks, in Mecklenburg county, about seventeen miles from the scene of the murder. He was brought back by private conveyance the entire distance to the place of the murder by the posse that had been in pursuit of him for two days and nights, which posse was composed of a large number of the most daring, fearless, and determined men of three counties. If any lynching was to be done these men who had spent sleepless nights, and travelled hundreds of miles, and freely spent their money to capture the fiends, certainly would have had the work to do. Yet, after delivering the prisoner into the hands of the officers of the law, they quietly went to their homes and to rest. It is true that the guards became frightened and carried the prisoners to jail during the night, but this fright was caused by the gathering of persons who had not been in the chase, and were not posted as to the intention of the majority and who have since assured the writer that they only came to learn what course had been decided upon and to lend their assistance if needed. It would have been an easy matter at many times to have lynched the murderers, and the bare fact that they were not so dealt with is positive proof that course was not the intent of the citizens, the many exaggerated reports to the contrary notwithstanding.

The writer assured the Sheriff that only he (the Sheriff) and two deputies were needed to bring the prisoners from Petersburg and safely land them in Lunenburg jail for trial. He also assured the military while they were on the trip to Lunenburg (as one who knew whereof he spoke) that there was not the slightest danger of violence at the hands of the citizens, and at various times during the trial he endeavored to impress it upon the military that the Commonwealth would be allowed every opportunity to punish the guilty parties. All of this the sequel has proved to have been true.

WOULD HAVE BEEN SAFE.

After the conviction the judge was assured that the prisoners would be just as safe from mob violence in the Lunenburg jail as at any other place in the United States; that the people only demanded that the prisoners be safely kept and not allowed to be turned loose upon the community again before the day of execution.

From the hour of his capture, on every occasion, Solomon Marable implicated the two women, Mary Abernathy and Pokey Barnes, in the murder of Mrs. Pollard. It is true he differed in his several statements as to the manner in which the murder was committed, but he steadfastly adhered to his first declaration as to the persons engaged in the act until Thursday evening, the 18th of July (one month to a day after he was captured). At this time Solomon had been tried and convicted. Mary Abernathy had also been tried and convicted, partly on the testimony of Solomon, corroborated by many circumstances. And let it be added right here that if Solomon Marable has ever told the truth in his life (in the opinion of the writer) he did so in his testimony in the trial of Mary Abernathy. Being assured of his speedy execution, all

The Latest News Gleaned From Various Parts of the States.

Charles Ringo, of Huntington, who was tried at the recent term of the Criminal Court, charged with the killing of one of his little step-children, and was released, and who is now indicted for the killing of the other one, made a confession. He states that his wife; the mother of the two little boys, killed them and threw their bodies into the river. He states that he was an eye-witness to the terrible affair, but the reason he did not divulge this before was on account of his love for the woman. He said that now since she was trying so hard to convict him he was going to give the whole affair away. He exhibits some letters which have some bearing on the subject. He says she took the children to a fleet of timber just below the wharf, and after strangling them threw them into the river. The authorities are working on the case and Mrs. Ringo will probably be arrested. She proclaims her innocence.

John B. Minor, LL. D., professor of common and statute law in the University of Virginia died Monday.

Mr. Minor was eighty-two years of age, having been born June 9, 1813; in the county of Louisa. His early education was acquired at Kenyon College, Ohio. Later he pursued academical and legal studies at the University of Virginia. Leaving the University, he resided first in Bedford county and then in Albemarie, at whose bar he begun the practice of law, with his brother, the late Lucian Minor.

The jury in the Massey-Pilot libel suit rendered a verdict in favor of Massey, awarding him damages to the amount of $1,600. The amount claimed for alleged damages was $50,000. The verdict is against Sam Small, and R. E. Byrd and the Pilot Newspaper Company, clearing the directors of the Pilot. The suit grew out of publications in the Pilot, then edited by Sam Small, formerly well known as an evangelist, charging bribery against Masses, who is superintendent of public instruction of Virginia, in connection with the State's dealings with what is termed the American-School-Book Trust. The libel suit was on trial twenty nine days.

Messrs. Wise and Flournoy, of Richmond, who have undertaken the task of securing a new trial for Mary Abernathy and Pokey Barnes, have gone to work in earnest. They are certain of the innocence of the women. It is said that a prominent white citizen has sent Mr. Wise $25 towards defraying the expenses that will be incurred, and from another white gentleman $10 was received.

Mrs. William Pierce of Middleport, N. Y., and her married son, Franklin, who own a large family boat and travel by river, operating a merry-go-round, were drowned at Cerelo. Mrs. Pierce while walking on the rear of the boat accidentally fell into the river. Her son jumped in to rescue her and the current swept them both under a float of barges lying just below. Both bodies were recovered.

John Hick's house at Big Stone Gap was burned. Four of his children were burned to death and his wife and one more child were badly burned. It caught from a stove and burned very rapidly while the family slept. The fire was not discovered until it was too late to do more than save the parents and one child on the lower floor.

Upon the construction of the phrase "Works of Necessity" depends whether in the future Richmond shall be a strictly moral city on the Saltbath. Chief of Police Howard in a public letter states that in view of the fact that a newsdealer has taken an appeal as to the enforcement of the Sunday closing law in his business that no arrests will be made until the decision of the Hustings Court has been given on this subject, but that a list of every newsdealer who keeps open on Sunday will be kept, and if the court's decision is favorable to the Commonwealth each will be summoned to show cause why he should not be fined for a violation of the law. The same action will be taken as to the street-car companies, and, in fact, as to every business conducted on Sunday, with the single exception of the sale of medicines.

The city attorney has given his opinion in regard to the matter, but it amounts to little more than quoting the law, as he does not say what constitutes works of necessity. In concluding his opinion the city attorney said: "I am of opinion that in attempting to enforce this law you should have no other guide except what you believe to be demanded by the need, habits and views of the people of this State."

Major Derbyshire Compliments the Men in His Official Report.
COUNSEL MAKE A STATEMENT.
Messrs. Wise and Flournoy Tett About Their Visit to Lunenburg- Evidence to Be Written Out-Feeling in the County.
Major J. H. Derbyshire, who was in command of the troops sent to Lunenburg to protect the negroes charged with the murder of Mrs. Lucy Jane Pollard, has forwarded his report to the Governor through the proper military channels. The paper deals entirely with the duties assigned the military, and the manner in which these duties were discharged. In view of the great sensation that this case has created, the report will prove of special interest just now. It is as follows:

RICHMOND, VA., July 24, 1895.
The Adjutant, First Regiment Infantry, Virginia Volunteers:
Sir.—I have the honor to report that, pursuant to orders No. 51, Headquarters First Regiment Infantry, Virginia Volunteers, July 11, 1895, I, in command of Companies A and B, First Regiment Virginia Volunteers, proceeded to the Danville depot in this city, and there reported to the Sheriff of Lunenburg county, Va., for his orders, which he gave me in writing, and as follows:

RICHMOND, VA., July 11, 1895.
Major J. H. Derbyshire, Commanding:
Sir.—You are hereby ordered to furnish me escort and safe guard for the prisoners under my charge from Richmond, Va., to the jail of Lunenburg county, and while there to use such means as may be necessary with your command to prevent said prisoners from being taken from my custody or the custody of those to whom I may commit them, and to continue to furnish such escort and guard until duly relieved by me.

In the execution of this order you will use such discretion as may seem to you necessary.

M. C. CARDOZO,
Sheriff Lunenburg county, Va. Witnesses:
necessary. M. C. CARDOZO,
Sheriff Lunenburg county, Va.
Witnesses:
Charles J. Anderson, Adjutant-General.
Henry C. Jones, Colonel.

THE PRISONERS TAKEN UP.

With the prisoners under escort, and accompanied by the Sheriff and two deputies, we left Richmond at 12:05 A. M., July 12th, reached Meherrin depot at 8 A. M., left Meherrin at daybreak, and arrived at Lunenburg Courthouse, at about 9:30 A. M.

The three prisoners were immediately placed in jail, and guard lines established. The prisoners during the trial were conducted to and from the court-house by a detail under command of Captain F. W. Cunningham, Company B, and this detail remained on duty in the courthouse while the trial were in progress. On the evening of July 15th and the morning of July 16th, I became more and more convinced that additional troops were necessary, and I therefore telegraphed to that effect, whereupon Company D, First Regiment Virginia Volunteers, under command of Captain Charles Gasser, was sent and arrived at Lunenburg Courthouse, about 5 A. M., July 17th.

HAD THE DESIRED EFFECT.

The effect of the arrival of this company was all that could be desired, for it could then be plainly seen that we were fully able to protect those under our charge.

The trials were concluded at about 11:30 P. M., July 20th. I thereupon received the following order from the Sheriff of Lunenburg county, Va.:

The committee brought with them the following full report of the mass-meeting held at Lunenburg Courthouse Tuesday, which they were delegated to have published in the Richmond papers, and which others papers are asked to copy:

At a meeting of the citizens of Lunenburg county, held at the court-house on August 6th, E. J. Gregory was called to the chair, and Walter Williams elected secretary. The committee on statement of facts made report that they had not completed said statement, and desired further time in which to do so. A letter from J. W. Overby, one of the committee to visit the city of Richmond, was read to the meeting, the sentiments endorsed, and the letter ordered to be published. On motion, the committee of six heretofore appointed, was reduced to two, consisting of H. C. Gregory and George E. Smith.

The following preamble and resolution were offered and unanimously adopted:

OTHER RESOLUTIONS.

Whereas, on the 14th of June last a most diabolical murder was committed in our county near the Charlotte line, by which Mrs. Lucy J. Pollard, a most estimable lady, was brutally butchered in her own yard between the hours of 4 and 6 o'clock in the afternoon of that day, as has been proved by sworn and reputable witnesses; and, whereas, our people, after earnest effort, succeeded in capturing and bringing to trial, without violence to them, the perpetrators of the crime; and the said parties having been given a fair trial under the law, by our County Court and by four trial juries selected principally from a distance of about twenty-five miles from the scene of the murder, and composed of our best citizens, white and colored, who testified under oath that they could give the prisoners a fair and impartial trial, and the said prisoners—viz. Solomon Marable, Mary Abernathy, Pokey Barnes, and Mary Barnes (the first three as principals in the murder, and the last-named as accessory)—were convicted and sentenced, the principals to be hung, and the last

THE CALL FOR MULTIARY.
whenever before the trial o
part of our people, but which was plainly evident during the trial was unnecessary, as the people were quiet and peaceable, and no desire shown or demonstration made on the part of the people during the trial to do violence to the prisoners, and while more troops were called for during the trial by the officer in command, we understood they were needed to relieve those already here, some of whom wore sick and all overtaxed by constant guard duty, and we understand that the officers in command stated to some of our citizens while the trial was in progress that they thought the troops were not needed, and we believe the officers themselves will certify that there was no danger during the trial of these prisoners of their being lynched by the citizens of the county.

And, whereas, after these prisoners were sent to Richmond, some of the press of the city, especially The Times, published to the State and country that the women had been convicted on the evidence of Solomon Marable alone, and were not guilty, and characterized our people, the juries included, as a lawless mob, seeking to execute innocent prisoners on the evidence of "Solomon Marable alone, who wasn't worthy of belief on oath," although by his confession alone he had been condemned to death, and in the same paper is quoted Solomon Marable's statement that "a white man had killed Mrs. Pollard, and had taken him along to witness the murder, and said paper uses Marable's statement as a basis, it seems, for an unwarranted attack on our county and people, and to advertise them as a lawless mob, incapable of according a fair trial to murderers who had partly confessed the crime; and as The Times and its reporters have undertaken to review the entire case, and persists in defaming and misrepresenting our county and people:

LOW ABIDING PEOPLE.

Therefore, be it resolved by the people of Lunchburg, in mass-meeting assembled, That we claim to be a law-abiding people, as evidenced by the fact that there has never been a lynching within the borders of our county; and we denounce the publications as not only false and unjust to us, but as dangerous to law and order, as it persists in publishing false theories and garnished statements from its own correspondents, or from a source which it acknowledges to be unworthy of belief, and withholds from the public the facts and the evidence as stated and published elsewhere by sworn witnesses and citizens, whose veracity cannot be impeached. We believe the press, when conducted on a high plane, free from prejudice or venality, to be a great bulwark of liberty and of law, but when used, as lately done in one of our Virginia cities, to bring false charges against the highest officers of our State, and thereby to force them, at great expense, into court to prove their innocence, and as in this instance, to publish the people of an entire county of the State as a lawless mob, because they have convicted two or three murderers on evidence considered sufficient by sworn juries of good citizens, we think it time for the people to be the censors of the press, and not for the press to be the censors of the people. If the officers in command of the troops sent to this county have caused these charges to be published by reporting it as their opinion on returning to Richmond, that these prisoners were not fairly tried, as we have some reason to believe, we regret it very much, as our sheriff requested their presence, and we have ever favored the maintenance of an ample State militia, to be properly used when needed, to protect criminals from mob violence, to suppress riots, and to assist the civil officers, when requested by them, in executing the laws, but we claim that they have no right, directly or indirectly, to interfere with the execution of the orders of the courts, or to the meting out of justice to criminals under the verdict of a jury, and if they are permitted to do so, it is best for the liberties of the people that the State militia be abolished.

A PROTEST.

We don't object to the acts of our court or the verdicts of our juries being reviewed in the proper manner and by the proper authorities, if it should be necessary, but we protest against this unwarrantable attack upon us, and the persistent efforts of the Richmond Times, or its reporters, to pervert the truth by suppressing the facts in our behalf and suggesting false theories in order to clear legally-convicted murderers, and to have innocent citizens tried for crime, or subjected to slander and expense, which they are unable to bear, and we call upon our
in the Richmond press, we are not allowed to be attended, many of the best citizens tried for crime, or subjected to slander and expense, which they are unable to bear, and we call upon our people, of every county in the State, to note the source from which these charges come, as it is the most potent means, if heeded, to encourage lynch law, as we must and will protect our wives and daughters without law, if legally-convicted criminals are allowed to go unpunished by technicalities in law, or by the assistance of a prejudiced or venal press, and we trust the press and people of every section of the State will join us in this protest.

The following, offered by Mr. E. J. Gregory, was also adopted:

In referring to the Richmond press, we are not alluding to the Richmond Dispatch. We believe that the Dispatch is a friend of our people, and we appreciate its attempt to deal fairly, and especially its efforts in to-day's (Tuesday's) paper to bring the true facts before the public.

This was followed by the adoption of this resolution:

Whereas, we have reason to believe that the said prisoners and convicts are under bad influence in the Richmond jail, we most respectfully request the proper authorities that the said prisoners be removed to some other jail pending the petition of a new trial.

The following were also adopted:

Resolved, That the thanks of this meeting and all the people of Lunenburg be, and are hereby, tendered to the editor of the Blackstone Courler for his noble and manly defence of Lunenburg in his issue of August the 1st, against the slanderous and libellous publications of a part of the Richmond press as to the trial of the Pollard murderers.

Resolved, That the thanks of the meeting are gratefully tendered to Mr. H. C. Gregory for the good work he has done in getting unp evidence and facts in the Pollard murder case.

The meeting was well attended, many of the best citizens of the county being present.

E. J. GREGORY,
Chairman.

WALTER WILLIAMS, Secretary.

event-2.A10:
THE LUNENBURG TRIALS.
A Criticism of Them-Some Remedies Proposed.
It has been of old determined upon every consideration of reason, justice, and religion, that lynchings contrary to law constitute one of the greatest blots upon American civilization; nor shall it be my province in this brief communication to reconsider the grounds of that decision. My purpose is to call the attention of the thinking public to an atrocity of a far blacker type, and that is, lynchings according to law, and I use the term advisedly.

A very short time since a murder was committed in Lunenburg county, and three negroes—a man and two women—were indicted for the crime. (Subsequently another woman was indicted for the crime.) Excitement ran so high after the arrest of the accused persons, that they were conveyed to Petersburg for safe-keeping, and before and during the trial at Lunenburg Courthouse by a jury of that county two companies of militia had to guard them from mob violence. In an atmosphere of military repression, an atmosphere in which impartiality and deliberation could not exist, so true it is that inter arma legis silent; guarded by soldiers at night, blivouacked around the jail, conducted under military escort to and from the court-house, and surrounded by troops during the trial, these creatures, entitled to the same rights by virtue of the sacred guarantees of the Constitution, as the wealthy, powerful, and aristocratic, were put on trial for their lives. A motion for a change of venue was made and overruled, and surely, if such a state of facts as that then existing is compatible with a fair trial by an impartial jury of the vicinage. I am prepared to believe that the victims condemned during the revolutionary furies of France by the saintly Robespierre, received a fair trial, and that the judicial murders of Lord Jeffries were according to law.

The man was convicted of murder in the first degree. One of the women was then put on trial and quickly convicted of the same offence; then immediately followed the trial of the second woman, and by that time public sentiment was at such fever-heat that the press dispatches stated that all three would be lynched, were she acquitted. She, too, was condemned to die. The third woman, who, according to the theory of the prosecution, was the most guilty of the crowd, was then tried, and sentenced to ten years' in the penitentiary. She was either guilty of murder in the first degree or innocent, and this verdict was of a piece with the balance of the travesty. They had no counsel, though the judge tried to procure them counsel, save that a motion for a change of venue was made by counsel, and, when that was overrued, he retired from the case.

RIGHT TO COUNSEL.

The right to counsel in criminal cases, and a fortiori in capital cases is guaranteed by the Federal Constitution, and in the language of Judge Cooley, is a universal principle of constitutional law. One of the standing and justifiable reproaches to the common law was that in ordinary felony cases, down to the recent year of grace, 1836, the accused was not allowed to employ counsel, save under such barbarous restrictions, that the right was denied. Who can doubt this horrible stain upon our jurisprudence after reading Charles Reade's terrific arraignment of the system in his masterpiece, Griffith Gaunt. When Mrs. Gaunt is tried for the murder of her husband, and the court, as a great concession, offers to allow her counsel, explaining to her what her counsel might do, she, with native dignity, refuses to suffer an honorable man to be so handicapped in her defence and put upon unequal terms with his adversary, the prosecuting attorney, and throws herself upon her innocence and her God. It makes but little difference that the presiding judge and the prosecuting attorneys in these cases (there were two of them), may have attempted to act impartially. That these prisoners were condemned to die without counsel will be a lasting disgrace to the State.

The recital of the facts in these cases brings me to the deliberate conclusion that these convictions were lynchings according to law, and the guilt or innocence of the accused cannot affect the question in any way. The mob which was restrained from the extremity of violence by the presence of three companies of militia said in trumpet-tongue to the judge and jury: "Try these prisoners at once, and right here, and convict them, and if you do not take their lives under the forms of law, we will take them by the violation of all laws, human and Divine." Whenever you invest the people with the right to demand immediate trials and speedy convictions, and make of courts and juries passive instruments to execute their will, then the last citadel of constitutional liberty has been stormed, and the majesty of the law prostituted in a temple of justice at the dictates of a mob. It will not do to answer that speedy trials are necessary to prevent lynchings, and that such measures are demanded by the inefficient administration of criminal law. There can be no state of facts which justifies the entire subservience of court and jury to the mob, and vest in the latter that deliberation and discretion which in every well regulated government must reside in the former.

LYNCH LAW.

Lynchers are not actuated by regard for law, because they know that in their numbers is perfect safety, and that none who take part in that execrable subversion of law will be punished. Could they, or any one of them, be once made to feel the halter draw. I am persuaded that hens'-teeth and lynchings would be of an equal degree of scarcity. There can be no greater fallacy than to argue that respect for the law is inculcated by making its application conform to the popular will. To be preserved in its integrity and purity it must know no distinction, and yield to no command. 'Tis in itself a sovereign, and its supremacy must be zealously maintained. Both in Winchester, and in some measure in Staunton, this mockery was exhibited recently, and in the former place a negotr negro was put on trial for a capital offence four days after it was committed, and in that case during the trial militia had to guard him from mob violence. I believe firmly that justice should be swift and inexorable, but I am also of the equally strong opinion that no man should be tried for his life when public opinion is too strong to secure him a fair trial. It makes no earthly difference whether he is guilty or innocent, for if his guilt be the argument for such ultra-judicial proceedings, then the same argument can be invoked to defend the worst excesses

A Lunenburg Citizen Handles Mr. Saunders with Gloves Off. LUNENBURG COUNTY. VA.
LUNENBURG' COUNTY, VA.,
August 14, 1895.

Mr. Saunders first states that lynchings contrary to law constitute one of the greatest blots upon American civilization (in this we all agree), and next calls attention to a crime the atrocity of which is of a far blacker type, and styles this crime "lynchings according to law." That Mr. Saunders is a lawyer of ability is patent, but who constituted him judge and jury to try the people of Lunenburg for a far blacker crime than murder? Upon whose sworn testimony has he reached the "deliberate conclusion" that our court, our Commonwealth's Attorney, and forty-eight jurymen are guilty of this crime?

Had not Mr. Saunders better take a dose or two of his own medicine? He says "the recital of the facts in these cases brings him to the deliberate conclusion that these convictions were lynchings according to law." Pray, Mr. Saunders, where did you get the facts upon which to reach this "deliberate conclusion"? Did you listen to the testimony of the thirty-seven or more witnesses who testified in these several cases? Did you, or any one else under the heavens, ever see a stenographic report of the evidence in these cases, as it fell from the lips of the witnesses? Judging from your communication it is much more probable that you have gotten your facts from the columns of the Richmond Times, a paper which has so persistently misstated the facts in these cases to establish a pet theory of its own—viz., that a white man committed this murder—that the people of our county as a unit on last Monday, at our regular County Court, censured this paper in unmeasured terms, and unanimously decided to withhold all patronage from it until it apologizes for the great wrong done to the people of our county. Were not the court and the sworn jurors, before which alone the evidence in full in these cases was given, the best judges as to its weight and credibility?
WERE THE PRISONERS IN DANGER?
Mr. Saunders states that after the arrest of the accused persons excitement ran so high that two companies of militia had to guard them from mob violence. How does Mr. Saunders know that this had to be done? Is it conclusive that because a thing was done it had to be done? The people of this county deny that there was any necessity for two companies, or one company, or any force of militia whatever, to protect these prisoners from violence during the trial.
The people had ample opportunity to lynch these prisoners when the crime was first committed had they so desired, at which time all people know excitement is more apt to lead to extreme measures. Unlike Mr. Saunders, in reaching his conclusions, we propose just here to introduce a little testimony.
Certificate of Colonel J. W. Ellis (ex-Sheriff):
This is to certify as regards the lynching of the murderers of Mrs. Pollard, that in the opinion of the undersigned the danger point had been passed when they were safely landed in the Petersburg jail.
J. W. ELLIS,
Ex-Sheriff Lunenburg County, Va.

ORDERING OF THE MILITARY.

We will not attempt to censure Sheriff M. C. Cardoza for requesting the presence of the military. From his standpoint, he doubtless thought it was necessary. Sheriff Cardoza resided fifteen miles from the scene of the murder, and therefore could not have been expected to have been fully posted as to the sentiment of the people in that section. He is our new Sheriff, having just entered upon the duties of the office, and it was but natural for him to desire that the responsibility for the safety of the prisoners should be shared by others. He was assured that only himself and two guards were necessary to bring the prisoners from Petersburg and safely land them in the Lunenburg jail. Out of abundant caution the military were there, but not because they had to be there. To the personal knowledge of the writer, there was not the slightest danger of mob violence at any time during the trial, and it is here asserted, without the fear of successful contradiction, that, save the officers of the court, jurors, and witnesses, there was not present at any one time during the trials thirty white citizens of the county. The powerful mob we have heard so much about was only in imagination.

It is true that a motion for change of venue was made and overruled. And Mr. Saunders says: "Surely, if such a state of facts as then existed is compatible with a fair trial by an impartial jury of the vicinage, he was prepared to believe," etc. Without testimony, Mr. Saunders assumes a state of facts to exist which did not exist, and upon this crumbling stone for the chief corner-stone he has attempted to erect this grand structure. A Negro Threatened With Lynching Confesses His Crime.
A Negro Threatened With Lynching Confesses His Crime.

Otsego (Mich.), Aug. 19.—A colored man last night broke into the house occupied by a Mrs. Smith. After forcing her to give up some jewelry, the negro attempted to assault Mrs. Smith, but her screams frightened him away.

The thief was arrested at Plainwell this morning, and was identified by Mrs. Smith. A crowd gathered around the jail with a rope, and gaining an entrance, placed the rope around the negor's neck and hauled him from the negor's cell. As the noose drew tight the fellow lost his nerve, and confessed that he was the guilty party, giving his name as Sam Sheeler of Fort Wayne. He implicated two or three other negroes, whom he said could be found in a swamp near here, and a posse has gone out to search for them.

Many robberies have been committed recently by this gang.

The negro's accomplices were located two miles northwest of the town. The robbers are trying hard to escape, and many shots have been exchanged. All the neighboring towns have been notified and the miscreants will be killed if they do not surrender. There is still talk of lynching Sheeler, and he will probably be removed to Allegan for safe-keeping.

Special to the Indianapolis Journal.

MARION, Ind., Aug. 19.—Calvin Dean lives on the Jonesboro and Fairmount turnpike, and one of the toll-gates stands on his land. In order to avoid paying toll it has been his practice to let down the fence on each side of the gate and drive past it on his own property. The gatekeeper kept a memorandum of these trips until a bill of $447 was presented. Dean refused to pay, and suit has been filed in the Circuit Court to enforce payment.

SHELBYVILLE, Ind., Aug. 19.—Three years ago Mrs. Dr. J. W. Parrish, of this city, fell at Bethany Park and fractured her thigh. She never fully recovered. To-day she fell on her crutches in some way and injured herself so severely that she is thought to be dying from internal hemorrhage.

Miss Elva Nickols, sixteen years old, was kicked by a horse last night and her hip broken.

Unfortunate Twins.
Special to the Indianapolis Journal.

DECATUR, Ind., Aug. 19.—One week ago to-day the eight-year-old daughter of policeman W. Gerry was burned to death. To-day a twin brother fell from a tree, breaking both legs and back and will die.

Special to the Indianapolis Journal.

MUNCIE, Ind., Aug. 19.—A local grocer found a Sandwich Island rodent in a bunch

of bananas Saturday and it is likely the only member of the rat family that ever emigrated to this country. The little animal is peculiar, as its head resembles a squirrel with the regular rat tail and feet. It had devoured four bananas while making the trip. It will be kept as a show window attraction.
